module.title: First Conditional: Realistic Causes and Real-life Consequences
module.group: A2.3 - World Explorations, Stories & Bridge to B1
module.objective: Express realistic future possibilities, plans, and consequences using First Conditional sentences with 'if' and 'unless'.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Choices and Future Results
subModules.grammarFocus: First Conditional (If + Present Simple, will + verb)

content.summary: In this reading mission, you will explore how actions in the present create realistic results in the future. You will read short texts about daily plans, study habits, and everyday choices while learning how to use the first conditional correctly.

linguisticTarget.grammar: First conditional structures using If + Present Simple and will + base verb, plus negative conditions with unless.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Everyday terms related to causes, consequences, making predictions, and setting personal goals.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning texts for specific cause and effect relationships and skimming paragraphs to understand the main ideas.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of short A2 texts about everyday choices and consequences.
Locate specific details such as conditions and future results in reading passages.
Recognize and practice grammar patterns with the first conditional and unless.

contextWarmup.prompt: What happens in real life if you study hard for your English exam?
options: You will pass the test with a good grade.
You will forget all English words immediately.
You will sleep through the entire exam.
contextWarmup.explanation: Studying hard leads to passing the test successfully in real life.

rules: Base pattern: If + Present Simple, will + base verb. Example: If it rains, we will stay home.
The if clause can be at the beginning or the end. If it is at the beginning, use a comma. Example: We will miss the bus if we don't hurry. / If we don't hurry, we will miss the bus.
Use unless (= if not) for negative conditions. Example: Unless you study, you will fail. This means if you do not study, you will fail.
After will, always use the base form of the verb without to. Example: If she calls, I will answer.

commonTrap.explanation: Learners often put will in the if clause or forget to use the base verb after will.
commonTrap.wrong: If it will rain, we stay home. / If it rains, we will staying home.
commonTrap.correct: If it rains, we will stay home.

content.contractionsSubtitle: Observe how subjects and verbs smoothly merge in everyday English:

contractions.subject: I
contractions.exampleFull: If I have time, I will help you.
contractions.exampleContracted: If I have time, I'll help you.

contractions.subject: You
contractions.exampleFull: You will pass if you practice.

grammarFormulas.description: Assemble sentence blocks to practice conditions and consequences:

paragraphs: Leo has big plans for the weekend. He wants to go hiking in the mountains with his friends on Saturday. However, the weather forecast looks uncertain. Leo knows that if the weather stays sunny, they will have a fantastic time exploring the trails. If it rains, they will stay home and play video games instead. Leo wants to achieve his fitness goals this month, so he hopes the sun shines brightly.

His friend Sam talks to him about the trip. Sam says, unless Leo finishes his homework on Friday night, he will not join the hiking group. Leo realizes he needs to be realistic about his time. If he hurries and finishes his schoolwork early, he will secure the opportunity to go. He promises to work hard so he will not miss out on the adventure.

questions.explanation: After 'will', the sentence requires the base form of the verb without 'to'.

Will is reduced and contracted in fast spoken speech.
The consonant sound at the end of leave blends into early.
The middle vowel in camera is often dropped in natural conversation.

content.summary: Learn how to write clear first conditional sentences to connect realistic causes with real-life consequences. Master correct verb tenses, comma placement, and conjunctions like if and unless.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: If-Clause Structure
blueprintItems.example: If you practice every day, you improve your skills.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Main Clause Consequence
blueprintItems.example: You will pass the exam if you study hard.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Alternative Condition with Unless
blueprintItems.formula: Unless + Subject + Present Simple, Subject + will + Base Verb
blueprintItems.example: Unless you leave now, you will miss the train.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use a comma after the if-clause when it starts the sentence.
mechanicsRules.badExample: If it rains tomorrow we will stay inside.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay inside.
mechanicsRules.why: A comma separates the conditional clause from the main clause when the conditional clause comes first.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always use the base verb form immediately after will.
mechanicsRules.badExample: If she wins the race, she will wins a trophy.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: If she wins the race, she will win a trophy.
mechanicsRules.why: Modal verbs like will must be followed by an infinitive without to.

mechanicsRules.rule: Do not use will in the if-clause.
mechanicsRules.badExample: If you will see Tom, tell him the news.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: If you see Tom, tell him the news.
mechanicsRules.why: The present simple tense is used in the if-clause, while will belongs in the main clause.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 1: Predicting Weather Consequences
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three sentences using the first conditional to describe what you will do based on different weather conditions.
guidedLabChallenges.example: If it is sunny tomorrow, I will ride my bicycle to the park. If it rains, I will stay indoors and read books. If it gets very cold, I will wear my warm winter coat.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 2: Study and Exam Success
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three sentences about studying and exam results using if and unless.
guidedLabChallenges.example: If I study every evening, I will get high grades on the math test. Unless I practice my vocabulary, I will struggle with the English quiz. If my friends need help, I will study with them.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Create a first conditional sentence from the given facts.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Combine these two facts using if: 'You practice piano.' -> 'You play well at the concert.'
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with 'If you practice piano...' and use 'will play'.
targetAnswers: If you practice piano, you will play well at the concert.
You will play well at the concert if you practice piano.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The present simple verb 'practice' goes in the if-clause, and 'will play' goes in the main clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'unless' instead of 'if not'.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Rewrite this sentence using 'unless': 'If you do not wear a coat, you will catch a cold.'
practicumQuestions.hint: Replace 'If you do not' with 'Unless you'.
targetAnswers: Unless you wear a coat, you will catch a cold.
You will catch a cold unless you wear a coat.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so the verb following it must be affirmative.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fix the capitalization, punctuation, and verb form where necessary.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Correct the errors in this sentence: 'if mark wakes up late he will miss his train.'
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalize the name Mark and the start of the sentence, and add a comma after the if-clause.
targetAnswers: If Mark wakes up late, he will miss his train.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Proper names and sentence beginnings require capital letters, and a comma separates the conditional clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write the correct present simple form of the verb in brackets.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Complete the sentence with the correct form of the verb in brackets: 'If Sarah (finish) her work, she will join us.'
practicumQuestions.hint: Sarah is third-person singular, so add -es to finish.
practicumQuestions.explanation: With third-person singular subjects (Sarah), present simple affirmative verbs take -s or -es.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Move the if-clause to the end of the sentence.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Rewrite this sentence by moving the if-clause to the end: 'If we hurry, we will catch the bus.'
practicumQuestions.hint: Remove the comma when the if-clause is at the end.
targetAnswers: We will catch the bus if we hurry.
practicumQuestions.explanation: When the main clause comes first, no comma is needed before 'if'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fill in the blank using 'will' and the base verb.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Complete the main clause: 'If you drop the glass, it ____________ (break).'
practicumQuestions.explanation: First conditional main clauses require 'will' plus the base verb.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Choose the correct conjunction for the sentence.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Fill in the blank with 'If' or 'Unless': '________ you water the plants every day, they will die.'
practicumQuestions.hint: If they will die without water, which conjunction means 'if not'?
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if not', meaning 'If you do not water the plants every day, they will die'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the mistake in the main clause verb form.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Find and correct the error in: 'If it snows, we will going to build a snowman.'
targetAnswers: If it snows, we will go to build a snowman.
If it snows, we will build a snowman.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Will' is followed directly by the base verb without 'going'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a complete first conditional sentence expressing a negative condition.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Create a first conditional sentence from: 'not study hard' -> 'fail the exam'.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'If you don't' or 'If you do not'.
targetAnswers: If you do not study hard, you will fail the exam.
If you don't study hard, you will fail the exam.
You will fail the exam if you do not study hard.
You will fail the exam if you don't study hard.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Negative conditions in the if-clause use 'don't' or 'doesn't' with present simple.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Type the exact words that form the conditional clause.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Identify the if-clause in this sentence: 'They will be happy if they win the match.'
practicumQuestions.hint: Look for the part of the sentence that starts with 'if'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The conditional clause is 'if they win the match', which states the cause.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: First Conditional and Real-life Consequences

content.summary: This lab focuses on speaking clearly when using the first conditional to talk about realistic causes and future consequences. You will practice clause pausing, sentence stress, and natural rhythm.
content.audioGuidance: Keep your voice steady and clear. Pause slightly after the if clause before stating the result with will. Stress the main action verbs to make your meaning clear.

pillars.name: Vowel Clarity
pillars.target: Clear short and long vowels in conditional sentences
pillars.explanation: Pronounce words like miss, achieve, and regret with distinct vowel sounds so listeners understand your exact meaning.

pillars.name: Clause Pausing
pillars.target: Natural pause between the condition and result
pillars.explanation: Take a micro pause after the if clause, for example, saying 'If you study hard, [pause] you will pass the test.'

pillars.name: Sentence Stress
pillars.explanation: Place stronger vocal emphasis on modal verbs like will and key nouns like consequence, opportunity, and goal.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice that the main stress moves slightly when changing from the verb to the noun form.
The second syllable remains stressed in both the verb and noun forms.
The stress shifts to the third syllable in the adjective form.
The main stress moves to the fourth syllable when forming the adjective.

drills.targetText: If you study hard, you will achieve your goals.
drills.phonetic: /ɪf juː ˈstʌdi hɑːd, juː wɪl əˈtʃiːv jɔː ɡəʊlz/
drills.focus: First conditional structure and natural pausing
drills.hint: Pause slightly after the comma between the condition and result.

drills.targetText: Unless we leave right now, we will miss the train.
drills.phonetic: /ənˈles wiː liːv raɪt naʊ, wiː wɪl mɪs ðə treɪn/
drills.hint: Pronounce 'unless' with a clear short 'e' sound in the second syllable.

drills.targetText: I promise I will help you if you ask me.
drills.phonetic: /aɪ ˈprɒmɪs aɪ wɪl help juː ɪf juː ɑːsk miː/
drills.focus: Linking pronouns and modal verbs smoothly
drills.hint: Blend 'I will' into 'I'll' for natural spoken rhythm.

drills.targetText: You will regret it if you don't take this opportunity.
drills.phonetic: /juː wɪl rɪˈɡret ɪt ɪf juː dəʊnt teɪk ðɪs ˌɒpəˈtjuːnəti/
drills.hint: Stress the third syllable of opportunity clearly.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Pronounce the target sentence clearly, focusing on the vocabulary word 'consequence'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Pronounce the first conditional sentence with accurate grammar structure.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this sentence: If you practice every day, you will achieve your dreams.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: If you practice every day, you will achieve your dreams.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Practice correct syllable stress on the word 'opportunity'.

practicumQuestions.explanation: Stress the third syllable in opportunity clearly.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Use rising intonation on the condition clause and falling intonation on the result.

practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ənˈles juː liːv naʊ, juː wɪl rɪˈɡret ɪt/
